meaning.evidence: Mostly the original verbatim, so nearly every fact survives, but two swaps change sense: "wash 60 heaps of dishes in your dishwasher" for 60 loads, and "Give a stuff about the width of the flapper" for "Pay attention to".

sense.evidence: Several terms strain or take the wrong sense: "Give a stuff about the width" (the idiom is a negative, "couldn't give a stuff"), "60 heaps of dishes", "to ensure a beaut seal", "If any colour rocks up in the bowl".

authenticity.evidence: Word swaps dropped into US agency prose: "Take a squiz at your water usage", "save water and the folding stuff", "Give a stuff about"; no Australian would phrase it this way.

register.evidence: Far lighter than level 4: whole paragraphs left as written, e.g. "Leak detection and flow monitoring devices can help you identify leaks or alert you to irregular water use in a home".

tone.evidence: Because it is mostly the original, the helpful advisory tone survives, though "Give a stuff about" lands as oddly flippant.

flow.evidence: Readable since mostly original, with jarring inserts: "If any colour rocks up in the bowl after 10 minutes" and "to ensure a beaut seal and avoid leaks".

variety.evidence: The little slang there is leans on "dunny" in every toilet line: "Dunny Leaks", "dunny flappers", "dunny model".

essence.evidence: Recognisably the EPA guide, since it is mostly unchanged.

problems.quote: Give a stuff about the width of the flapper
problems.original: Pay attention to the width of the flapper
problems.why: "Give a stuff" is used in the negative ("couldn't give a stuff"); as a positive instruction it reads wrong and mildly rude.

problems.quote: wash 60 heaps of dishes in your dishwasher
problems.original: wash 60 loads of dishes in your dishwasher
problems.why: "Loads" (dishwasher cycles) swapped for "heaps", which changes the measure.

problems.quote: If any colour rocks up in the bowl
problems.original: If any color shows up in the bowl
problems.why: "Rocks up" is for people arriving, forced for dye appearing.

problems.quote: Leak detection and flow monitoring devices can help you identify leaks or alert you to irregular water use in a home
problems.original: Leak detection and flow monitoring devices can help you identify leaks or alert you to irregular water use in a home
problems.why: Largely untranslated, far below the level-4 brief.

A.summary: Mostly the untouched original with a few word swaps, several of them in the wrong sense.

meaning.evidence: All points kept, plus metric conversions as colour on the given figures: "more than 9,300 gallons (about 35,000 litres)", "Make sure you flush straight after the test so it doesn't stain the cistern."

sense.evidence: "dunny flappers", "cistern", "Have a squiz", "the folding stuff", "get onto an experienced handyman" all fit.

authenticity.evidence: Natural Australian plain speech: "Fixing the easy household leaks can knock about 10 percent off your water bills", "to help people get their heads around the upside".

register.evidence: A plain, lightly Aussie rewrite; much of it is standard English ("Leak detection and flow monitoring gadgets can help you find leaks"), lighter than a level-4 brief asks.

tone.evidence: Stays helpful and practical: "Tip: Don't forget to turn the water off at the line before you start!"

flow.evidence: Smooth throughout: "Check your water meter before and after a two-hour stretch when no water's being used. If the meter moves at all, you've probably got a leak."

variety.evidence: Varied enough, though "gadgets" recurs in the device section: "Leak Detection and Flow Monitoring Gadgets", "tips for picking a gadget".

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the EPA guide: structure, headings, tips and figures intact.

problems.quote: Leak detection and flow monitoring gadgets can help you find leaks or tip you off to odd water use at home
problems.original: Leak detection and flow monitoring devices can help you identify leaks or alert you to irregular water use in a home
problems.why: Close to the original phrasing; the text sits lighter than the level-4 brief overall.

B.summary: Clean, faithful and natural, with helpful metric conversions, but closer to level 3 than 4.

meaning.evidence: Every point and figure kept with conversions as colour: "send more than 9,300 gallons (around 35,000 litres) of water down the gurgler every year", "replace it at least every five years so it seals properly".

sense.evidence: "down the gurgler", "The usual suspects", "Have a squiz", "a once-over", "get onto an experienced handyman" all carry the right sense.

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like a local explaining it: "No word of a lie", "Swapping one over is a quick, easy fix that saves you water and the folding stuff."

register.evidence: A chatty Aussie retelling ("Good news is they're often easy to fix"), at about level 4, a touch restrained in the device section.

tone.evidence: Keeps the friendly, practical advice: "Tip: While you're at it, it's a good idea to check the washer or \"o\" ring inside the showerhead too".

flow.evidence: Reads naturally aloud, with one slightly topicalised line: "Pipe tape, also called teflon tape, you can get at most hardware shops".

variety.evidence: Varied: "No word of a lie", "The usual suspects", "Good news is", "Give the tap washers and pipe fittings a once-over", "While you're at it".

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the EPA guide retold, headings and tips kept.

problems.quote: Pipe tape, also called teflon tape, you can get at most hardware shops;
problems.original: Pipe tape, also called teflon tape, is available at most hardware stores
problems.why: Fronted object is a little awkward.

C.summary: A natural, faithful level-4 retelling that keeps the guide's practical tone.

meaning.evidence: Every fact and figure kept; additions are reactions to the original: "Every year!", "One little drip!", "like it's haunted", "or you'll be wearing it!", "Not bad for an arvo's tinkering."

sense.evidence: "down the gurgler", "easy as", "a bit suss", "keeping it ticking over", "if it hasn't gone walkabout", "don't muck about" all fit their contexts.

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like a real Aussie handyman: "the lot pays for itself in the water you stop chucking away", "then you go hunting for where the bugger's coming from".

register.evidence: A full level-4 voice ("Strewth, where do I start?") with swearing at dad level: "where the bugger's coming from".

tone.evidence: The helpful, practical advice comes through, though the frequent exclamations ("Every year!", "One little drip!") push it toward a jokey rant in places.

flow.evidence: Reads like spoken advice: "Check your water meter, then leave it two hours with nobody using a drop, and check it again."

variety.evidence: Varied slang, but the exclamatory asides are a noticeable tic: "Every year!", "One little drip!", "or you'll be wearing it!"

essence.evidence: Still clearly the EPA leak guide, every section and tip kept.

problems.quote: Not bad for an arvo's tinkering.
problems.why: Implies the fixes take an afternoon, a small claim the original does not make.
One of several exclamatory asides that become a tic.

D.summary: The liveliest and most authentic level-4 voice, keeping every fact; the exclamatory asides are slightly overused.

meaning.evidence: All points kept: "more than 9,300 gallons of water a year", "replace it at least every five years", though the last tip drops "at the line": "Don't forget to turn the water off before you get stuck in!"

sense.evidence: Most fit ("a doddle to fix", "clapped-out", "get stuck in"), but "save you water and a bit of coin" uses a US money term and "Suss out toilet leaks by dropping a few drops" strains.

authenticity.evidence: Mixes Aussie with US and British forms: "first you've gotta work out", "to help folks get their heads around", "a bit of coin", "a doddle", and keeps "Toilet Leaks" beside "dunny".

register.evidence: A chatty level-4 retelling ("track down where the bugger's coming from", "strewth!"), with vulgarity within dad level.

tone.evidence: Practical advisory tone kept: "Tip: While you're at it, it's a good idea to check and, if need be, replace the washer".

flow.evidence: Mostly smooth, with a repeat in "Suss out toilet leaks by dropping a few drops" and a tacked-on "That's enough water for more than 180 showers, strewth!"

variety.evidence: Reasonably varied ("chew through", "chucking away", "a doddle", "clapped-out", "get on the blower"), though toilet/dunny switches without pattern.

problems.quote: save you water and a bit of coin
to help folks get their heads around
That's enough water for more than 180 showers, strewth!
problems.original: That's the amount of water needed to take more than 180 showers!
problems.why: "Strewth" tacked on at the end feels bolted on.
Keeps "toilet" in headings while using "dunny" in the body, inconsistently.

E.summary: A decent level-4 retelling, faithful, but with a scatter of American and British forms.
